name: Argos
note: Inachos to Perseus to Herakles: the deepest documented line in the tree

Io.note: Priestess of Hera at Argos, loved by Zeus, and turned into a white heifer to hide her -- which fooled nobody. Hera set hundred-eyed Argos to watch her and then a gadfly to drive her over the whole world; the Ionian Sea and the Bosporos, the ox-ford, are named from her wandering. In Egypt Zeus restored her with a touch. Apollod. 2.1.3, Aeschylus PV 561-886

Epaphos.note: Born in Egypt at the touch -- epaphe -- of Zeus' hand that ended Io's madness. King of Egypt; the Greeks identified him with the Apis bull. Apollod. 2.1.3-4

Libye.note: Daughter of Epaphos, and the name Greece gave to all Africa. Apollod. 2.1.4

people.Belos: King of Egypt, son of Poseidon and Libye; father of the twin quarrel that runs the next three generations. Apollod. 2.1.4
people.Danaos: King of Libya, who fled to Argos with his fifty daughters rather than marry them to his brother's fifty sons -- the first sea voyage, the tradition says, and the first ship of fifty oars. Apollod. 2.1.4-5
people.Aigyptos: Brother of Danaos, father of fifty sons, and the man Egypt is named after. Apollod. 2.1.4

Hypermnestra.note: One of the fifty Danaids, and the only one who did not do it: told to kill her husband on the wedding night, she let Lynkeus live because he had spared her. Her forty-nine sisters carry water for ever in jars that will not hold it. Apollod. 2.1.5

people.Lynkeus: The one bridegroom of fifty who survived his wedding night, and the ancestor of everything that follows in Argos. Apollod. 2.1.5, 2.2.1
people.Abas: King of Argos, whose shield was so feared that waving it put down rebellions after his death. Apollod. 2.2.1
people.Akrisios: King of Argos, who was told by the oracle that his daughter's son would kill him and shut her in a bronze chamber under the ground to prevent it. Apollod. 2.2.1-2, 2.4.4
people.Proitos: Twin of Akrisios; they quarrelled in the womb and fought over Argos all their lives. Apollod. 2.2.1

Danae.note: Shut in the bronze room, and reached anyway: Zeus came to her as a shower of gold. Her father put her and the baby in a chest and threw it in the sea, and it came ashore on Seriphos. Apollod. 2.4.1

Perseus.note: Killed Medousa with Athena's mirror-shield and Hermes' sickle, took Andromeda from the sea-monster, and founded Mykenai. He killed Akrisios in the end with a discus at the games, by accident, exactly as the oracle said. Gives the constellation and the Perseid meteors. Apollod. 2.4.1-5

Andromeda.note: Chained to a rock as a sacrifice because her mother Kassiopeia boasted of being fairer than the Nereids. Perseus took her off it. Mother, grandmother and great-grandmother of the Argive kings, and a constellation beside her husband. Apollod. 2.4.3

people.Elektryon: King of Mykenai, son of Perseus, and father of Alkmene. Apollod. 2.4.5
people.Alkaios: Son of Perseus, father of Amphitryon. Apollod. 2.4.5
people.Sthenelos: Son of Perseus, father of Eurystheus -- who set the labours. Apollod. 2.4.5
people.Eurystheus: King of Mykenai, and the man Herakles had to serve: Hera hurried his birth and delayed Alkmene's so that the throne Zeus had promised to the next-born of Perseus' line went to him instead. He set the twelve labours and hid in a jar when Herakles brought the boar back. Apollod. 2.4.5, Il. 19.95-133

Alkmene.note: Granddaughter of Perseus, wife of Amphitryon, and mother of twins by two fathers in one night -- Herakles by Zeus, who came in her husband's shape and made the night three times its length, and Iphikles by Amphitryon, who came home the next day. Apollod. 2.4.7-8

people.Amphitryon: Son of Alkaios, exiled for killing his father-in-law by accident with a thrown club. Apollod. 2.4.6

Herakles.name: Herakles (Hercules)
Herakles.note: Glory-of-Hera, named for the goddess who spent his life trying to kill him: snakes in the cradle at ten months, madness that made him kill his own children, and the twelve labours as the penance for it. Roman: HERCULES, whom the Romans worshipped at the Ara Maxima and who is far more a working man's god at Rome than in Greece. Made immortal on the pyre at Oite and married to Hebe. Gives herculean, and the Pillars of Hercules at Gibraltar. Apollod. 2.4.8-2.7.7 After the pyre he was made immortal and married Hebe, Youth herself -- the reconciliation with the goddess whose name he had carried all his life while she tried to kill him. Theog. 950-955

people.Iphikles: Twin of Herakles by the mortal father, born the same night and entirely mortal. Apollod. 2.4.8
people.Hyllos: Eldest son of Herakles, and leader of the first attempt of the Herakleidai to take back the Peloponnese. Apollod. 2.8.1-2
people.Tlepolemos: Son of Herakles, who founded Rhodes and led its nine ships to Troy, where Sarpedon killed him -- one grandson of Zeus killing another. He fixes this line against the war. Il. 2.653-670, 5.628-662

Makaria.note: Daughter of Herakles, who offered her own life to win the Herakleidai their battle. Apollod. 2.8.1

people.Temenos: Great-great-grandson of Herakles, who took Argos in the Return of the Herakleidai eighty years after the war -- the event Greek historians used as their first fixed date. Apollod. 2.8.2-5
people.Kresphontes: Brother of Temenos, who took Messenia by a trick with the lots. Apollod. 2.8.4-5
people.Aristodemos: Brother of Temenos, whose twin sons took Sparta and founded its double kingship, which lasted into historical times. Apollod. 2.8.2-5
people.Iolaos: Nephew, charioteer and companion of Herakles, who burned the Hydra's stumps for him. Plutarch says male couples swore their vows at his tomb in Thebes. Apollod. 2.5.2, Plut. Erotikos 761d

unions.note: Fifty daughters; the tree keeps the one whose line continues, and the other forty-nine stand behind this record. Apollod. 2.1.5
Fifty sons, of whom one lived. Apollod. 2.1.5
Two fathers, one night, one birth: Zeus' ray to Herakles is drawn separately, and the mortal descent runs through Amphitryon here so that Herakles keeps his place in Perseus' line. Apollod. 2.4.8
The three brothers who divided the Peloponnese between them by lot. Apollod. 2.8.4
Their children are unnamed here on purpose: the sources differ on how many and give them no stories, and what is remembered is only how they died. Apollod. 2.4.11
Hera's priestess, pursued and turned into a white heifer to hide her, then driven over the whole world by a gadfly. Apollod. 2.1.3
Shut in a bronze room sunk under the ground by her own father, and reached there as a shower of gold. Apollod. 2.4.1
He came to her wearing her husband's face, on a night he made three times its length; she thought Amphitryon had come home early. Apollod. 2.4.8
